title: Explain XGBoost Tree Depth
prompt: Explain how maximum tree depth changes an XGBoost model's capacity, bias and variance, overfitting risk, and training and inference cost. Then describe how you would choose it in practice. State which other controls you would tune with depth and why. This is a writing exercise.

response.placeholder: Separate the capacity of one tree from the effective complexity of the full boosted ensemble.
response.reference_answer:
## Core answer

max_depth caps the depth of each tree. A larger value lets a tree partition the feature space more finely and represent higher-order interactions, so it usually reduces approximation bias but raises variance and the risk of fitting noise. XGBoost explicitly describes deeper trees as more complex, more likely to overfit, and more memory-intensive to train.

Deeper trees usually require more split-search work and memory during construction. At serving time, each tree can require a longer root-to-leaf traversal; actual cost also depends on the grown and pruned structure, tree method, hardware, and ensemble size.

## Choosing it

Treat depth as one part of the regularization plan. Use a validation split that matches the deployment time or population, select the metric before tuning, and use early stopping to choose the number of boosting rounds. Tune depth jointly with min_child_weight and gamma to constrain splits, reg_alpha and reg_lambda to regularize leaf weights, row and column subsampling to reduce variance, and eta with the number of rounds. A smaller eta makes each boosting step more conservative and normally requires more rounds.

## Caveat

The shortcut “deeper means lower bias and higher variance” is useful, but it is not a guarantee about one run. The ensemble's behavior also depends on shrinkage, the number of trees, sampling, split constraints, and the data.
